knowledge_type_note: A strategic principle with an unusually firm PRECONDITION attached, which is what stops it being merely a rule of thumb. Vukovic's tradition holds that an attack is not a choice of style but a consequence of an existing advantage.

attributions.note: The doctrine that one must not attack without an advantage is his; Lasker summarised his theory as 'Do not attack when you have no tangible advantage in position.'
The Art of Attack in Chess is the standard systematic treatment; focal points and the conditions for the classic bishop sacrifice are his.

history.notes: Attacking the king is as old as chess; what is attributable is the doctrine that it requires justification (Steinitz) and its systematic treatment (Vukovic). Neither is a claim of invention. Vukovic's text has not been read directly — see the source's access caveat.

development.change: Attack treated as the normal way to play; soundness a secondary question.
Attack becomes conditional on an existing advantage rather than a matter of style.
Systematised: preconditions, timing, focal points, pawn-shelter types, named sacrifices.
Defensive resources better understood; the third opposite-castling scenario — attacking while also slowing the opponent — becomes the common treatment.

engine_era_note: Engines have raised the bar for what counts as a justified attack, refuting many attacking sacrifices that were played on general grounds, and have made defence look far more resilient than classical writing assumed. The PRECONDITION doctrine survives this well; what does not survive is the romantic assumption that a king with a damaged shelter is losing.

preconditions: More attacking units bear on the king's sector than defending units, or the king's cover is durably weakened
The attacker's own king is safe, or safe enough for the time the operation needs
The centre is closed or under control, so a counter-blow there is not available
indicators_for: A clear focal point — a weak square next to the king that pieces can occupy or sacrifice on
The defender's key defensive piece (often a knight on f6 or a fianchettoed bishop) can be exchanged or driven off
A file or diagonal can be opened towards the king by a pawn break
Opposite-side castling, so pawns can advance without cost
A hook — an advanced enemy pawn that gives the attacker something to attack in order to open a line
indicators_against: The centre is open or can be opened by the defender
Development is unfinished; a missing rook is often the exact tempo the attack lacks
The defender can trade queens, which usually ends the attack
The attacker has no way to bring a third piece to the sector
The king's shelter is intact and there is no sacrifice that breaks it
recognition.detector: lib/matchers.js: king-attack, implementing all three of the record's preconditions. The repository's `kingAttack` puzzle tag (checks >= 2 or mate) remains a proxy for puzzle classification and is NOT this.
false_positive_traps: Two checks is not an attack. The repository's `kingAttack` tag fires on checks >= 2 or mate, which is a proxy for puzzle classification and NOT a definition of the concept.
An exposed king is not automatically under attack — with the attacking pieces traded off, an exposed king is often just an active one. This is a registered false-positive case.
Advancing pawns at a king is not an attack unless pieces can follow into the lines that open.

typical_plans: Exchange the defender — the f6 knight, the g7 bishop — before striking
Open a file or diagonal with a pawn break, then double heavy pieces on it
Sacrifice on a focal point to strip the shelter, with a follow-up piece already in range
In opposite-side castling, count tempi to contact and start the storm first
Combine the attack with prophylaxis against the opponent's counter-attack
typical_moves: Bxh7+ and Bxh6 sacrifices on the shelter
Rook lifts to the third rank and across
typical_pawn_structures: f7-g7-h7 intact — most resistant, usually needs a sacrifice
f7-g6-h7 — holes on f6 and h6, but sound while a bishop sits on g7
f7-g7-h6 — h6 is both a target and a hook for g4-g5
typical_piece_arrangements: Queen and bishop battery on b1-h7
Rook on the g- or h-file behind an advancing pawn
tactical_consequences: Mating nets, sacrifices on focal points, forced king walks
strategic_consequences: An attack that fails usually leaves the attacker structurally worse, especially after a pawn storm

exceptions: An attack without a positional advantage generally fails; this is the doctrine's core and it is a genuine constraint, not encouragement.
A wing attack can be refuted by a central counter-blow — the standard antidote.
Trading queens usually ends an attack, so the defender's simplest defence is often to seek that trade.
Damaged pawn cover is not decisive by itself. It matters in proportion to the attacking force that remains.
limitations: Recognition confidence is LOW. 'Local superiority near the king' is a judgement about which pieces count, and no mechanical detector in this repository attempts it.
The repo's kingAttack tag is a puzzle-classification proxy and should not be read as the concept.
Fires on 12 of the 788 shipped positions (1.5%). It is a claim that the PRECONDITIONS for an attack are met, never that an attack exists, and the difference is why the confidence is capped at low.

Adams-Kasparov 2005 after 21...Kxh7 is the registered case it must refuse: opposite-side castling, a pawn storm arrived, the shield gone, two rooks on the files at the king - and no attack, because only one piece bears on the king's zone and White's own king is the one being mated. It refuses.

MEASURED 2026-09-01: the shipped puzzle generator tags 134 of the 788 positions `kingAttack` and this base reports the concept on 12. The gap is the record's own first false-positive trap made numeric - the generator's test is `checks >= 2 or mated`, which is a proxy for sorting puzzles and not a definition, and a two-check sequence is not an attack. Recorded rather than reconciled: moving either number toward the other would mean one of the two systems telling a lie it does not currently tell.
misconceptions: That attacking is a matter of temperament. The classical position is that it is a consequence of an advantage you already hold.
That an exposed king is losing.
That pushing pawns at the king is an attack. Without pieces to follow, it is a structural concession.

conflicts.resolution: Directly opposed for the same pawn moves: advancing the g- and h-pawns attacks and simultaneously exposes your own king. Opposite-side castling resolves the conflict (the pawns are not in front of your king); same-side castling does not, and there the burden of proof is on the attacker.

counterexamples.note: Adams-Kasparov, Linares 2005 (round 12), Kxh7. Human ground truth: the concept is named for this position by Jon Speelman (GM), reproduced by ChessBase; the king-safety sentence is quoted from a community annotation and is corroborated, not relied on. Corpus entry `adams-kasparov-2005-21Kxh7-king-attack-negative`, which carries the full annotation, the alternates the annotator rejected, and the engine's verdict. Every mechanical sign of a winning king attack is present - opposite-side castling, a pawn storm that has arrived, the shield gone, two rooks on the files pointing at the king, a bishop on g5 and a queen able to reach h6 - and the attack does not exist. This is the sharpest kind of negative example because nothing about the pattern is missing; what is missing is a threat, and a threat is a propert

engine.verdict_note: fully, and it agrees with the named human move. Searching the position AFTER 21...Kxh7, Stockfish 18 at depth 22 returns Be3 - the move Speelman names as White's best - and scores it at -2.13 from White's side. The side with the 'attack' is two pawns worse. Searched from White's move rather than Black's, because the claim being tested is about the position the recapture reaches, not about whether the recapture was forced.

counterexamples.note: Registered false-positive case `an-exposed-king-with-nothing-left-to-attack-with`, kept on the record as well as in tests/false_positive_cases.json so that the concept carries its own negative evidence. THE SURFACE PATTERN IS PRESENT: The black king on g8 has no pawn cover at all — no f-, g- or h-pawn in front of it. An exposed king looks like a king under attack. WHY IT IS NOT THE CONCEPT: This record's own trap: "An exposed king is not automatically under attack — with the attacking pieces traded off, an exposed king is often just an active one." Both sides have one rook and one pawn. There is nothing left to attack with, and the same is true of White's king. WHAT THE SYSTEM DOES: The API does not report king-attack. The matcher requires attacking pieces bearing on the king zone rather than an absence of pawn cover, which is what the trap asks for. Stockfish 18 at depth 28: +0.00 in a fully symmetric position — the exposure is mutual and neither side can do anything with it. The related trap on the same record, that the repository's `kingAttack` tag fires on two checks or mate and is a puzzle-classification proxy rather than a definition, is why the matcher does not read that tag here.

by_level.beginner: White is bringing more pieces near the black king than Black has defending it, and trying to open a line to get at it.
by_level.intermediate: An attack on the king. It works here because {more attackers than defenders / the shelter is weakened} — and note the centre is {closed / controlled}, so there is no counter-blow.
by_level.advanced: The attack is justified by {local superiority / a focal point on {square}}. The critical question is the defender's key defensive piece and whether it can be removed.
by_level.master: Count attackers against defenders in the sector, identify the focal point, and check the centre and the queen trade before committing. The doctrine since Steinitz is that an attack must be earned, not chosen.

by_depth.short: More force is bearing on the king than is defending it.
by_depth.normal: An attack on the king, justified by {reason}. Attacks require a pre-existing advantage — usually more pieces near the king than the defender has, or holes in the pawn cover — and they fail when the centre is open or the defender can trade queens.
by_depth.deep: Vukovic's treatment is the standard one. An attack is a consequence of an advantage rather than a choice of style, a doctrine going back to Steinitz. It is usually best understood as an operation against a specific weak square next to the king — a focal point — rather than against the king in general. The pawn shelter's type matters: f7-g7-h7 intact is the most resistant and normally needs a sacrifice; f7-g6-h7 has holes on f6 and h6 but is sound while a bishop stands on g7, which is why trading that bishop is so often the whole plan. Opposite-side castling turns the game into a race where a tempo decides, and the modern treatment combines attacking with slowing the opponent down rather than pure racing.

explanations.lesson: Before attacking, count: how many of your pieces can reach the king's sector, and how many of theirs defend it? If the answer is not in your favour, improve the position instead — and check the centre first.

beginner_words: opening a line to the king
avoid: attack because the king looks exposed

definition_short: A concerted operation against the enemy king, justified only by an existing advantage — usually local superiority in force near the king, or weaknesses in its cover.
definition_long:
Not a mood but a consequence. The classical position, following Vukovic, is that an attack must be EARNED: you cannot attack the king without a positional advantage, and attacking without one fails against any competent defence. The advantage usually takes the form of LOCAL SUPERIORITY — more pieces bearing on the king's sector than the defender has defending it, or a pawn majority there — or of durable weaknesses in the king's pawn cover.

FOCAL POINTS. Vukovic's central contribution: 'every focal-point is a weak square in the defender's territory and a potentially strong one for the attacker', especially when adjacent to the king. g7 and h7 (g2 and h2 mirrored) are the classic ones. An attack is usually best understood as an operation against a specific square rather than against the king in general.

PAWN COVER. The three common shelters differ sharply in resilience. f7-g7-h7 unmoved is the most resistant and usually has to be broken by sacrifice. f7-g6-h7 leaves f6 and h6 as holes and invites h4-h5 or f4-f5 to open a file — but is not weak while a bishop sits on g7, which is why exchanging that bishop is so often the whole plan. f7-g7-h6 gives the h6 pawn as a target and a hook for g4-g5.

OPPOSITE-SIDE CASTLING changes the character completely: pawns can be thrown forward without exposing one's own king, and the game becomes a race where a single tempo decides. Franco distinguishes three scenarios — a mutual race, an attack against pure defence, and the modern treatment that combines attacking with prophylaxis on one's own wing.

The standing counter-principle is that a wing attack is answered in the centre. An attack launched while the centre is open, or while one's own development is unfinished, tends to rebound.
